segments.text: Today I'm showing you how I keep my sourdough starter healthy without fussing over it every day.
A starter is just flour and water colonised by wild yeast and lactic acid bacteria.
The yeast makes the bread rise, and the bacteria give it that sour flavour.
I feed mine at a one to one to one ratio: one part starter, one part flour, one part water, by weight.
Weigh everything. Cups are wildly inconsistent with flour.
After feeding, mark the level on the jar with a rubber band.
At room temperature a healthy starter doubles in about four to eight hours.
It's ready to bake with at its peak, when it's domed and full of bubbles.
If you see a grey liquid on top, that's called hooch. It just means the starter is hungry.
Pour it off or stir it in, then feed it. Stirring it in makes the flavour more sour.
If you don't bake often, keep the starter in the fridge and feed it once a week.
Take it out the day before baking and give it two feedings to wake it up.
Whole rye flour gives the starter a big boost because it has more nutrients for the microbes.
The only real reason to throw a starter away is pink or orange streaks, which mean bad bacteria.
Normal sour or even slightly vinegary smells are fine.
So: feed by weight, watch it double, use it at the peak, and the fridge is your friend.

facts.fact: Fridge + weekly feeding if baking rarely
Pink/orange streaks mean throw it away
